summaries.example: Imagine a lamp with two bulbs. A switch chooses which bulb can receive power. If the power is turned on, the room becomes bright. Did turning the switch cause the room to become bright? Maybe not: either bulb could have lit the room. But if the left bulb were broken, turning the switch to the right would seem important. This shows why philosophers ask what exactly a cause changes.
summaries.summary: The metaphysics of causation asks what we mean when we say that one thing caused another. Philosophers first separate particular cases from general patterns. One particular drought causing one famine is a token claim. Saying that drowsy driving causes crashes is a type claim. They also distinguish constants, such as events or facts, from variables, such as how much a plant grows. Causation is used for relations between constants, while influence is used for relations between variables. Even these labels are debated. Some philosophers think causes are events; others think they are facts or variable values. They also disagree about absences, such as a failure to water a plant. Examples with backups, prevention, switches, and ordinary versus unusual conditions show that simple rules about causes can run into trouble. The entry examines what causes and effects are, how finely they should be described, and how causal claims may be represented by models.
key_ideas: Causal claims can be about particular happenings or about kinds of happenings.
Philosophers disagree about what causes and effects are: events, facts, or values of variables are some suggestions.
An absence can sometimes seem to be a cause, such as not watering a plant.
A cause does not always have to be necessary. A backup cause might have produced the same effect.
The way we describe a situation can change which cause seems important.
Some philosophers study influence between changing amounts or choices, such as how watering affects plant height.
summaries.why_it_matters: We use cause-and-effect ideas to explain accidents, make predictions, and decide what changes might help. Careful thinking can show why two people may describe the same situation differently. It also reminds us that a simple story about “the cause” may leave out backup possibilities, background conditions, or the exact way an outcome happened.

important_terms.definition: A particular thing that happens, such as one drought, one famine, or one window breaking.
A general kind of thing or event, such as droughts or car crashes in general.
The thing that brings about another thing, or is said to do so.
The thing that happens as a result of a cause.
A question about what kinds of things really exist and how they are related.

questions_to_think_about: If two things happen at the same time and place, must they be the same event?
Can not doing something, such as not watering a plant, be a cause?
If two people could each make a window break, who caused it when only one acted?
Is making a difference the same as being a cause?

summaries.example: Consider the two-bulb switch case. Filipa moves a switch so that power will reach the right bulb, while Phoebe turns on the power. Both actions are needed for the right bulb to light, and the right bulb lights the room. Yet it is tempting to say that Phoebe caused the illumination while Filipa caused only the way it occurred. If the left bulb were broken, however, Filipa’s action would also seem to cause the illumination. The intrinsic process from Filipa’s action to the light has not changed; what changes is the counterfactual situation. This challenges simple accounts of causation and raises questions about transitivity.
summaries.summary: The metaphysics of causation investigates what causal claims commit us to and what makes them true. A central framework distinguishes tokens from types and constants from variables. A particular drought causing a particular famine concerns token causation; a general claim about drowsy driving and crashes concerns type causation. Claims about how one variable affects another are classified as influence. The proposed relata of token causation include events, facts, and variable values. Each option raises questions about absences, identity, and fineness of grain. If two descriptions have different causal consequences, one might infer that they refer to different relata, but this can produce extremely fine-grained, even hyperintensional distinctions. Alternatives include treating causal language as explanatory or intensional, or analyzing causation as involving contrasts. Cases of preemption, prevention, double prevention, and switching test theories based on processes, probabilities, regularities, counterfactuals, and interventions. Normality may help distinguish causes from background conditions. Type causation has several possible relationships to token causation, and a general cause can have a net effect distinct from an effect along one particular causal path. Formal causal models represent influence with structural equations or probabilistic systems, while the metaphysical question remains what makes such models accurate or appropriate.
key_ideas: The entry distinguishes token causation, type causation, token influence, and type influence.
Candidate causal relata include events, facts, and variable values; each proposal faces questions about identity and level of detail.
The causal-differences argument says that if two descriptions differ causally, they may denote different relata. Critics respond with causal explanation, intensionality, or contrastive causation.

Preemption shows that a cause need not be necessary for its effect, since a backup could have produced the effect. Prevention and double prevention create different problems for process-based theories.
Switch cases suggest that causation may depend on counterfactual alternatives and may not be transitive in the ordinary two-place sense.
Type causation may be reduced to patterns of token causation, may explain token causation, or may be treated as equally fundamental. Net effects and path-specific component effects can come apart.
summaries.why_it_matters: Causal reasoning is central to science and ordinary explanation, but the entry shows that “X caused Y” can hide several different claims. Distinguishing tokens, types, variables, contrasts, pathways, and background conditions helps clarify disagreements. It also explains why prediction or intervention may depend on how a model groups possible values and which alternatives it holds fixed.

important_terms.definition: A particular occurrence used as a causal relatum, such as one person’s smoking or one cancer case.
A general kind or pattern used in a causal claim, such as smoking or cancer in general.
An entity that stands in a causal relation, such as an event, fact, or variable value.
A changing quantity or question, such as how much someone weighs; its value is one possible answer or state.
A formal relation between variables, often represented in a causal model.
A claim about whether an occurrence would change if another occurrence were different or absent.
A causal case in which one potential cause blocks or takes the place of another potential cause.
The idea that a causal claim may depend on what it is contrasted with, not merely on cause and effect alone.

questions_to_think_about: Does a token causal claim require a corresponding type causal regularity?
Should an omission count as a cause, or only as an enabling condition?
Do different contrasts make one and the same event causally different?
Can a causal model be accurate even if it idealizes a system as deterministic?
What should count as the cause in a switch case: the power, the switch, the bulb, or a combination?

summaries.example: Suppose a student forgets to water a classroom plant, and the plant dies. It is natural to say the forgotten watering caused the death. But what exactly was the cause? Was it an event—the student’s not watering? A fact—that the student did not water? Or a variable value, such as the amount of water the plant received? Now imagine that another student had promised to water it but also forgot. We may blame the broken promise more readily than the other student’s silence. Philosophers ask whether this difference comes from what really caused the death or from what we normally pay attention to.
summaries.summary: This entry studies the underlying structure of cause-and-effect claims. It distinguishes particular cases, called tokens, from general kinds, called types. It also separates constants, such as events and facts, from variables, such as how much a person weighs or how much a plant grows. The proposed relations between constants are called causation, while relations between variables are called influence. These terms organize the discussion, but philosophers disagree about whether all of these relations really exist and whether one can be explained in terms of probabilities, regularities, counterfactuals, processes, or something else. For token causation, major candidates for the relata include events, facts, and variable values. Questions about omissions, the level of detail in an event, and different descriptions of the same occurrence create difficult cases. Preemption shows that a cause need not be necessary, while prevention raises questions about whether a cause must be connected by a physical process. Switches can make causation appear non-transitive. The entry also examines type causation, net and component effects, and formal models of influence using structural equations and interventions.
key_ideas: A statement about one drought and one famine differs from a statement about droughts and famines generally.
The entry uses “causation” for relations between constants, such as events or facts, and “influence” for relations between variables.
There is no agreement about whether causes and effects are events, facts, variable values, or other entities.
Absences are controversial: not watering can seem to cause a plant’s death, but some philosophers deny that absences are genuine causes.
Preemption, prevention, and switching show why necessity, probability, and a simple chain of events may not fully explain causation.
Normal background conditions can be hard to separate from causes, and philosophers disagree about whether this difference is objective or depends on our interests.
summaries.why_it_matters: Understanding causation affects how we explain what happened and how we decide what would happen under a change. The distinctions in this entry help separate several questions that ordinary language blends together: what happened, what kind of pattern exists, which alternatives matter, and what a model represents. That care is useful whenever a conclusion depends on identifying a cause.

important_terms.definition: One specific occurrence, such as this student’s forgetting to water this plant.
A general category or pattern, such as forgetting to water plants.
A thing that can stand in a causal relationship, including an event, fact, or variable value.
A question or quantity that can take different values, such as how much water a plant receives.
A general relationship in which one kind of variable changes another, often studied with a model.
A situation where a possible backup cause would have worked if the actual cause had not occurred.
A condition that allows a cause to work but may not itself be singled out as the cause, such as oxygen for a match.
A formal representation of influences among variables, sometimes using equations or diagrams.

questions_to_think_about: Is saying “smoking causes cancer” just a summary of many particular cases?
Can one event have different causal descriptions depending on the contrast being considered?
Why might a backup cause fail to count as the actual cause?
Are oxygen and a match-strike equally causes of the match lighting?
What information should a causal model leave out, and what must it preserve?
